probe.limits: What this model leaves out: daylight hours use the geometric definition, so there is no atmospheric refraction and the Sun is treated as a point. That makes each day about 6 to 15 minutes shorter than a sunrise-to-sunset table gives, depending on latitude; at 51.5 degrees north the model says 16 h 24 m at the June solstice against about 16 h 38 m published. The Earth is a smooth sphere: no terrain, no mountains, no time zones, and the globe turns at the sidereal rate with an arbitrary starting phase, so the longitude under the Sun is not the real one for a given clock time even though the latitude of the sub-solar point is. The Sun is a parallel light source, so its angular size, the twilight band and eclipses are absent. The orbit is the two-body approximation from the JPL table: the distance, the declination and the date of perihelion are from that table, and the table is only valid from 1800 to 2050.
probe.describe: Earth on 20 Jun 2026. The sub-solar latitude is 23.4 degrees, so the Sun is overhead at 23 degrees north. 52 degrees north gets 16 h 24 m of daylight. The Earth is 1.0162 AU from the Sun, 1.62 percent from its mean distance. Paused.
